title: Two-Step Sign-In
about: Add a second lock to your accounts so a password alone isn't enough.

cards.prompt:
Even a great password can be stolen, when a website gets hacked or when you type it into a fake one.

Could a **stranger far away** get each of these?

items.label: A password stolen in a website hack
A password you typed into a fake website
Your pet's name, which you posted online

cards.explanation: Things you **know or type** (passwords, answers you've posted) can be stolen and used from anywhere. Your **phone** and your **fingerprint** stay with you. That's why asking for one of them as well makes an account much harder to break into.
cards.hint: Ask of each one: is it information that could be copied and sent anywhere, or a thing that is physically with you?
cards.nudge: Anything that's just information can be copied from far away. Things in your pocket, or part of your body, can't.

cards.title: Two-step sign-in
cards.body:
**Two-step sign-in** (also called **two-factor**) asks for a password **plus** a second proof, like your phone or fingerprint. A stolen password alone can't get in.

Sign-in methods, strongest first:

- A **[[passkey]]**: your device checks your fingerprint, face or PIN. Fake sites can't use it.
- A code from an [[authenticator app]].
- A **text code**: scammers can sometimes steal phone numbers.

cards.prompt:
A **sign-in code** is the second key to your account. A site sends one when someone types your password. **Nobody real ever asks you to send them a code**: not a company, a bank, a game or a friend.

You're watching a video when your phone buzzes.

steps.text: A text arrives: **"Your sign-in code is 481 902."** You weren't signing in to anything. What does it probably mean?

choices.text: Someone knows my password and is trying to sign in
choices.consequence: Right. The code stopped them, but they have your password.
Codes are sent when someone tries to sign in. Someone tried, and it wasn't you.

steps.text: A minute later, a message from a friend's account: **"Oops, I sent you my code by mistake! Can you send it back?"**

choices.text: Send the code, to be helpful
choices.consequence: That was the attacker. The code was for **your** account, and now they're in.

choices.text: Don't send it. Change your password, and warn your friend another way
choices.consequence: The attacker has no way in, and your friend learns their account was taken over.

cards.explanation: A code you didn't ask for means someone has your password: **change it**. Never send a sign-in code to anyone, even a friend. Their account may have been taken over.
cards.hint: Codes arrive when someone tries to sign in. And remember the rule: nobody real ever asks you to send them a code.

cards.prompt: Put these ways to sign in in order, from **strongest** to **weakest**.
cards.explanation: A **passkey** is strongest, then a password with an **authenticator app**, then a password with a **text code**. A password alone is the weakest: one leak and it's open.
cards.hint: Sign-in methods were listed strongest first. And any second proof beats none.
cards.nudge: A password with any second proof beats a password on its own. Among the second proofs, think about which one scammers can sometimes steal.

cards.prompt: You're setting up a new music app. For two-step sign-in, it only offers one option: **codes by text message**.

steps.text: Text codes are the weakest kind. Do you turn two-step sign-in on, or skip it?

choices.text: Turn it on: a weaker second lock still beats having none
choices.consequence: Right. Anyone with just your password is now stuck without the code.

choices.text: Skip it: text codes can be stolen, so they're not worth it
choices.consequence: Stealing a phone number takes real work, and most attackers only have a password. A text code still stops them.

choices.text: Skip it for now, and wait until the app offers passkeys
choices.consequence: That could take years, and until then your account has only one lock. Turn on what's offered now.

cards.explanation: Any second proof beats none. Turn on the strongest one a site offers, even if that's text codes, and switch to a better one if it's added later.
cards.hint: Compare a password plus a text code with a password on its own. Which is harder to break into?

cards.prompt:
A **password manager** is an app that makes a long random password for every account, remembers them all and fills them in. You remember just **one main passphrase**. It only fills in on the **real** website, never on a fake one.

Sam has 40 accounts. Which plan keeps them safest?

options.text: A password manager, locked with a strong passphrase and two-step
One very strong passphrase, used for all 40 accounts to keep it simple
options.nudge: A strong password used everywhere has the same problem as a weak one: one data breach opens all 40 accounts.

options.text: A different easy password for each one, like game1, game2, game3
options.nudge: A pattern like this is quick to guess, and one leaked password shows the pattern for the rest.

cards.explanation: A **password manager** gives every account its own long random password, so one leak can't open the rest. Sam only has to remember one strong passphrase, and two-step sign-in guards the manager itself.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the other 39 if one password leaks.

cards.prompt: Match each one to what it does.

pairs.right: Remembers a different password for each account
A second proof as well as your password
Signs you in with your device and fingerprint, face or PIN
A one-time number sent when someone signs in

cards.explanation: A **passphrase** is long and memorable, a **password manager** keeps one password per account, **two-step sign-in** adds a second proof, a **passkey** signs in with your device, and a **sign-in code** is a one-time number sent when someone signs in. Never share it.
cards.hint: Start with the ones you're surest of. Two of them are about remembering passwords, and three are about signing in.
cards.nudge: A passphrase is something you make up; a password manager is an app. A code is sent to you, just for one sign-in.

cards.prompt:
When you turn two-step sign-in on, the site gives you **backup codes** to save somewhere safe, in case you lose your phone.

Months later, your phone, with your authenticator app on it, falls in a lake.

steps.text: You try to sign in on a laptop, and it asks for the code from the app. What can you use?

choices.text: One of the backup codes you saved when you set it up
choices.consequence: You're in. Now set two-step sign-in up again on your new phone.

choices.text: Ask the website to switch two-step sign-in off for good
choices.consequence: That leaves your account with one lock. Use the backup codes you saved.

choices.text: Ask someone online who says they can get you in
choices.consequence: Anyone offering to get into accounts for you is a scammer.

cards.explanation: That's why you save **backup codes** when you turn two-step sign-in on. Keep them somewhere safe, like in your password manager or printed at home.
cards.hint: When you turned two-step sign-in on, it gave you something to save for exactly this moment.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **Two-step sign-in** adds a second proof, so a stolen password isn't enough.
- **Never share a sign-in code.** An unexpected one? Change your password.
- A **password manager** remembers every password and won't fill in fake sites.

That's your accounts locked. Next module: spotting scams.
